name: Nose bone massaging / nasal bone pushing
lead: Nose bone massaging, or nasal bone pushing, is a bonehacking practice in which a person presses or massages the nose, usually the bridge, in the belief that this can narrow it, straighten it or change its shape without surgery. Practitioners aim for a slimmer, more refined bridge and better facial harmony, and the practice sits in the 'softmaxxing' end of looksmaxxing, which avoids surgery and injectables.[5] It needs no equipment, only the hands, and is usually described as something done daily over weeks or months.

The nasal bones are two small paired bones forming the bridge of the upper third of the nose, joined at the midline and attached to the frontal bone and maxilla.[1] The visible shape of the nose also depends on cartilage and skin: the upper lateral cartilages support the middle third, the lower lateral cartilages form the tip, and the skin of the lower third is thicker and less mobile.[4] Because shape and size vary so much between individuals, the nose is a frequent focus of facial-harmony discussion.[1]

The practice spread through the same online ecosystem as mewing and other non-surgical 'bonehacks', which Wikipedia traces to incel and PSL forums in the 2010s and to TikTok in the early 2020s.[5][7] Medical literature on the nasal bones deals almost entirely with fractures, their reduction and surgical correction, and with rhinoplasty.[2][3][4] No published study has tested whether pressing or massaging the nose reshapes it in healthy people.
infobox: Narrowing, slimming or straightening the nose

paras: The practice consists of applying pressure or massage to the sides or bridge of the nose, usually over a period of weeks or months, with the intent of nudging the nasal bones toward a narrower or straighter position. It is grouped with other bonehacks, which are non-surgical attempts to change facial bone structure; the better-known examples are mewing and the much-publicised, rarely practised 'bonesmashing'.[5] Variants described by practitioners include gentle squeezing of the sides of the bridge, stroking or pressing along the bridge, and routines combined with other facial exercises.

Shape and size of the nasal bones vary widely between individuals, and most nasal bones can be loosely described as V-shaped or S-shaped, although these are not medical categories.[1] The two bones meet at the internasal suture and articulate with the frontal bone, the maxilla, the ethmoid and each other.[1]

The visible form of the nose also depends on the cartilage framework below the bones: the upper lateral cartilages, the lower lateral cartilages that form the tip, and the septal cartilage, which surgeons reshape in rhinoplasty.[4] Surgeons describe the nose as three layers, a bone-and-cartilage framework, a mucosal lining and skin, with skin thin over the bridge and thicker at the tip, where it can blur the outline of the cartilage underneath.[4] The bridge is the bony upper third, while the cartilaginous middle and lower thirds shape tip and apparent width.[4]

Wikipedia's account of looksmaxxing places its roots in the PSL forums, PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net, in the 2010s, with spread to TikTok in the early 2020s, where non-surgical routines were often framed as self-improvement.[5] Softmaxxing is described there as minor, non-invasive improvements such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness, with mewing the best-known bonehack.[5] Mewing was named after the British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike, and Google Trends interest in the term rose from January 2019.[7]
Nasal bone pushing has no documented originator or dated first description; it is a folk practice that grew up alongside other bonehacks.

Practitioners hold that sustained, repeated pressure could remodel bone and cartilage gradually, in the way that orthodontic forces move teeth, and some say they have seen the bridge become narrower or straighter over months.
Experts and medical sources describe the nasal framework in the context of injury and surgery, and no published study has examined whether routine massage alters it.[2][3][4]

Rhinoplasty is the surgical operation for reshaping the nose and is listed among the cosmetic surgeries pursued under 'hardmaxxing' in Wikipedia's account of looksmaxxing.[4][5] Wikipedia notes that swelling after open rhinoplasty can take at least a year to diminish and that revision rhinoplasty occurs in roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations.[4] Nose reconstruction has a long history, from the Edwin Smith Papyrus to John Orlando Roe's first modern closed rhinoplasty in 1887, with the open approach introduced by Rethi in 1934 and popularised in the 1970s.[4] A #NoseJobCheck trend spread on TikTok in early 2021.[4]

Closed reduction, manual realignment of a recently fractured nasal bone by a clinician, is the one setting where hands-on repositioning of the nasal bones is established medical practice; Wikipedia states it is usually performed within about 10 days of injury in adults, before the bone heals misaligned.[6]

No studies found on massage or pressure as a method of reshaping the uninjured nose. Clinical research on the nasal bones concerns trauma. Isolated nasal fractures are described as the most common injury of the central midface [2], and reviews note that management of fractures varies widely between surgeons [3]. A review in the German literature states that closed reduction can be offered for misalignment once swelling has subsided, and that rhinoplasty or septal reconstruction is considered no earlier than 6 to 12 months after the injury if results are insufficient [2]. These sources concern injured noses, not routine massage.

Surgical studies describe how deviated or fractured nasal bones can be repositioned by a clinician (closed reduction) or by rhinoplasty, which is a procedure performed by trained surgeons rather than self-applied pressure.[2][3][4]

Trauma reviews emphasize that injury to the nose requires exclusion of septal hematoma or abscess, which need emergency surgical treatment; Wikipedia gives septal hematoma as occurring in about 5 percent of nasal injuries.[2][6] These findings relate to injury, and no studies have measured the effects of self-applied pressure on the nose. Reports about the related practice of bonesmashing describe facial surgeons warning about fractures, facial misalignment, neurovascular injury and vision changes, and Wikipedia describes bonesmashing as an inside joke that is rarely carried out.[5]
Gentle massage is a different activity from the forceful practices those warnings address, and no source documents harms specific to it.

Coverage of looksmaxxing in outlets such as The Guardian (February 2024), the BBC (March 2024) and Business Insider and The New York Times (November 2023) has focused on bonesmashing, mewing and cosmetic procedures; nasal massage is generally a minor item within that coverage.[5] Doctors quoted in coverage have criticised mewing and bonesmashing as misinformation, and a December 2025 paper advised physicians to help patients distinguish safe beauty practices from harmful ones.[5]

lore.intro: Nose-pushing is discussed as one of the zero-cost 'softmax' routines alongside mewing, and is usually shared as short videos or forum posts rather than as a documented protocol.[5]

claims.claim: Repeated pressure on the nasal bridge can narrow or straighten the nose over months.
claims.believers: Practitioners say gradual pressure remodels the bone or cartilage.[5]
claims.experts: No published study has tested massage or pressure on healthy noses; clinical literature on nasal bones concerns fractures and surgery.[2][3]

claims.claim: Cartilage is soft enough to be moved by hand even if bone is not.
claims.believers: Proponents point to the cartilaginous middle and lower nose as the part most able to shift.[4]
claims.experts: Surgeons describe the cartilage framework as something reshaped operatively in rhinoplasty; no study examines massage of it.[4]

claims.claim: Bonehacks like nose pushing are a safe alternative to rhinoplasty.
claims.believers: Softmaxxers favour them because they avoid surgery, cost and recovery.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes rhinoplasty swelling can last a year and revisions occur in roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations; it describes no equivalent data for massage.[4]

claims.claim: Forceful pressure or hitting the face (bonesmashing) sculpts bone.
claims.believers: Wikipedia describes it as hitting the face with objects such as a hammer to create a 'chiselled look'.[5]
claims.experts: Facial surgeons warn of fractures, misalignment, neurovascular injury and vision changes, and sources label it misinformation and a rarely practised joke.[5]

claims.claim: Manual repositioning of the nasal bones works.
claims.believers: Practitioners point to the fact that clinicians can reset a broken nose by hand.[6]
claims.experts: Closed reduction is done by clinicians on fresh fractures, typically within about 10 days in adults, and is not a treatment for an uninjured nose.[6]

claims.claim: Nose pushing can be part of a broader facial-harmony routine with mewing.
claims.believers: Community members combine it with tongue-posture and jaw routines.[5][7]
claims.experts: Researchers argue evidence that mewing changes facial structure is lacking, and the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence of it improving the jaw.[7]

card.summary: Pressing or massaging the nose to narrow it; no study supports reshaping and medical literature covers only fractures.
card.note: Nasal injury literature shows damage needs professional assessment.

quick.overview:
Nose bone massaging is a bonehack in which people press or massage the nose, usually the bridge, hoping to narrow or reshape it.

No clinical study has tested this on healthy noses; the medical literature on nasal bones is about fractures and surgery.
quick.mechanism: Proponents' idea is that repeated pressure moves the nasal bones or the structures around them. Anatomy sources describe a bone-and-cartilage framework that surgeons reshape operatively, and none has examined massage.
quick.risks: No studies have measured the effects of self-applied pressure on the nose. Trauma reviews note that injured noses need assessment for septal hematoma, which requires emergency treatment.

chain: Repeated pressure or massage applied to the nasal bridge
Claimed gradual remodeling or narrowing of the bones
A slimmer or straighter-looking nose, according to practitioners
angle.text: People press or massage the nasal bridge hoping to slim or straighten it without surgery. The shape of the nose is set by bone, cartilage and skin, and surgeons reshape it through rhinoplasty.
